Create trajectories

a03_trajectories.Rmd

Before generation

The analyst defines the target cohort and the clinical state cohorts. The target interval supplies the observation bounds. State intervals determine when a patient belongs to each clinical state, including any history states. Cohort2Trajectory applies the configured selection and transition rules to these intervals. It does not infer clinical history, episode duration or observation coverage.

Complete the configuration and data import before calling createTrajectories(). Use the same studyEnv throughout the workflow.

getDataForStudy(cdm = cdm, studyEnv = studyEnv)
trajectories <- createTrajectories(cdm = cdm, studyEnv = studyEnv)

For local data, omit cdm and configure useCDM = FALSE. A failed import blocks generation until another import succeeds. Previously saved patient files are not used as a substitute for that failed import.

Discrete trajectories

Discrete trajectories assign one state to each fixed-length cycle. Set lengthOfStay to the number of calendar days per cycle. Despite its name, this argument is a cycle length, not a hospital length of stay. For example, use seven days for weekly trajectories:

trajectories <- createTrajectories(
  cdm = cdm,
  studyEnv = studyEnv,
  trajectoryType = "Discrete",
  stateSelectionType = "Priority",
  lengthOfStay = 7
)

Cycles begin at the target start date. Both ends of a cycle are included, and the last cycle is shortened when the observation boundary falls before a full cycle ends. The example uses the priority order already configured in studyEnv.

The three selection methods choose among states that overlap the cycle and are allowed by the transition rules:

Method Selection within a cycle
"First" Choose the interval with the earliest start date, including intervals that began before the cycle. Resolve equal start dates using the priority order.
"Overlap" Choose the state covering the most distinct days in the cycle. Combine separate intervals for the same state without counting overlapping days twice. Resolve equal coverage using the priority order.
"Priority" Choose the highest-ranked state present during any part of the cycle.

List every clinical state in stateCohortPriorityOrder, with the highest priority first. This is required for all three discrete methods. Priority is a ranking, not a way to exclude states from the analysis.

With mergeStates = TRUE, overlapping source intervals are composed into states with structured membership during import. Selection then uses those resolved states and their inherited rules, including any explicit merged-state overrides. See Configuration for the merging rules.

Use the names "Discrete", "Continuous", "First", "Overlap" and "Priority" for these settings. Names are case-insensitive. Numeric choice codes are not accepted by the public functions.

Continuous trajectories

Continuous trajectories use calendar intervals rather than fixed cycles. lengthOfStay does not determine their timing.

trajectories <- createTrajectories(
  cdm = cdm,
  studyEnv = studyEnv,
  trajectoryType = "Continuous",
  stateSelectionType = "Priority"
)

In continuous mode, "First" and "Overlap" have the same behavior. They retain the bounded input intervals that pass the transition rules, including overlapping intervals. They do not perform the cycle-level comparisons described above.

Continuous "Priority" assigns shared days to the highest-priority state that the transition rules permit. Lower-priority intervals can be shortened or split into separate fragments. Every clinical state must appear in the priority order. Continuing the same selected interval does not require a new self-transition each time an unrelated record starts or ends.

Continuous output does not extend a state across an undocumented gap. Simultaneous records keep their dates and equal elapsed times. Their ordering in the table is not evidence that one event occurred earlier within that day. A downstream model that requires distinct event times needs an explicit tie-handling rule.

Transition rules and gaps

An empty allowedStatesList allows unrestricted transitions. Otherwise, each state used as a transition source needs one named entry containing all its allowed destinations. Use character(0) for a source with no allowed destinations. Source names must match the state labels exactly. Destination matching is case-insensitive. The first clinical state and the START and EXIT boundary markers do not need an incoming transition rule. For merged studies, a nonempty list must include every original state, including absorbing states. Use character(0) for an original state with no permitted destinations.

Rules are applied separately for each patient, using the last retained clinical state. A rejected record does not become the source for later transitions. In discrete mode, only allowed states compete for the cycle. In continuous mode, prohibited records are excluded before the absorbing-state cutoff.

When no state can be selected for a discrete cycle, oocFix controls the result:

  • "None" or "OUT OF COHORT" leaves the cycle as OUT OF COHORT.
  • "Last present state" carries the last selected state forward only when its self-transition is allowed. Before the first selected state, the gap remains OUT OF COHORT.
  • A state label supplies a named fallback, provided the transition to it is allowed. Use its exact spelling. For merged states, use the display label, not the internal state_key.

OUT OF COHORT means that no clinical state was selected for the cycle. It does not mean that the patient was unobserved. An unresolved cycle does not erase the last selected state when checking later transitions. The strings "None" and "Last present state" always select their gap-handling behavior, even if a clinical state has the same label. Gap handling applies only to discrete output.

Observation boundaries and absorbing states

The first target-cohort interval supplies each patient’s start and end dates. Patients with no clinical state records can still have trajectories if they meet the mandatory-state requirements. Their discrete cycles follow the gap rule. Their continuous trajectories contain the boundary markers without invented clinical intervals.

By default, state intervals are bounded by the target interval. With outOfCohortAllowed = TRUE, retained state records can extend its end, but not its start. Set this during import if those later records are needed. Changing it only at generation cannot recover records removed during import. Local input must include a target row for every patient to be retained during import.

Only a selected, allowed absorbing state can end the trajectory before its observation boundary. A prohibited or unselected absorbing record does not end follow-up. No further transition checks are made after a retained absorbing state.

For discrete trajectories, generation stops after the selected absorbing cycle. The row still uses the cycle’s dates, so it is not automatically shortened to the original event date. If the target interval itself ends on that date, the final cycle is shortened at that boundary. For continuous trajectories, follow-up ends at the retained absorbing interval’s end date. Earlier overlapping intervals are also capped at that endpoint.

START marks the trajectory start. EXIT marks the day after the last retained cycle or the continuous follow-up endpoint. These markers do not add observed time and do not, by themselves, indicate death.

Clinical history and event timing

History belongs in the analyst’s state definitions. For example, separate absorbing states for death with and without a prior pneumonia history can retain that distinction in the selected terminal state. Cohort2Trajectory does not construct that history classification from the state labels.

A selected history-specific death state preserves the category, but it does not recover exact event timing from a discrete cycle. If pneumonia and death occur within one weekly cycle, the output may contain only the selected death state. Its cycle dates do not reveal the pneumonia onset date, the interval between the events or whether they occurred on the same day. Changing the selection method does not make the weekly table a complete event log.

Continuous trajectories and the cleaned interval files provide different timing detail. Selection, target-boundary clipping and state merging can still affect those intervals. See Trajectory output for the output fields, date conventions and available files.

Saved studies and output

For a fresh study, generation settings can be supplied directly as in the examples above. Mandatory-state requirements are an import decision. To change them, rerun getDataForStudy() with the intended requirements before generating trajectories.

A completed fresh run saves Settings/analysisSettings.rds in the current version 4 format. It contains the analysis settings and, for CDM studies, the cohort definition contents used by the successful import. It does not contain patient data. Only version 4 snapshots are accepted. Older snapshots must be recreated by completing import and generation with the current package.

After configuring a study with runSavedStudy = TRUE, import fresh data and use the restored analysis settings without overrides:

getDataForStudy(cdm = newCdm, studyEnv = studyEnv)
trajectories <- createTrajectories(cdm = newCdm, studyEnv = studyEnv)

Saved CDM runs use the definitions embedded in the snapshot, not the current working JSON files. Saved local runs use fresh local input. Configure a new study if the analysis rules need to change.

createTrajectories() returns a data frame and saves it in the study’s Data directory. The trajectory CSV is written after all patient batches finish, so a batch error does not replace it with a partial result.

With useCDM = TRUE and a supplied CDM object, generation joins age and gender from the CDM. This can also be requested after importing local cohort data. With useCDM = FALSE, age and gender_concept_id are present but contain NA. No birth date is assumed. The output article describes the full schema and how to interpret these columns.
